questions.stem: A decision problem X is in NP iff:
choices: There is a polynomial-time certifier C(I, t) such that I is a yes-instance iff there exists a poly-length t with C(I, t) = YES
X is solvable in subexponential time
questions.explanation: NP = problems with short, polynomial-time-checkable certificates of YES.

questions.stem: Y is NP-complete iff:
choices: Y is in NP AND every X in NP reduces to Y
questions.explanation: NP-complete = in NP and NP-hard (every NP problem polynomial-time reduces to it).

questions.stem: The Cook-Levin theorem proves which problem is NP-complete?
questions.explanation: Cook-Levin establishes that any NP problem's certifier can be encoded as a SAT/CIRCUIT-SAT instance, making it the first NP-complete problem.

questions.stem: If any NP-complete problem is in P, what follows?
questions.explanation: Polynomial algorithm for an NP-complete problem composes with reductions to solve every NP problem in P, giving P = NP.

questions.stem: Which is NOT a standard canonical NP-complete problem?
questions.explanation: Bipartite Matching is in P via max-flow. The others are NP-complete.

questions.stem: What is the certificate for Vertex Cover (decision form)?
choices: An edge subset of size k
A vertex subset S of size k; certifier checks every edge is incident to S
questions.explanation: Certificate is the candidate cover; certifier verifies size and edge incidence in polynomial time.

questions.stem: Independent Set <=_p Vertex Cover is which type of reduction?
choices: Simple equivalence (S is IS iff V \ S is VC)
questions.explanation: Simple set-complement duality: (G, k) -> (G, n - k).

questions.stem: Hamiltonian Cycle <=_p TSP uses what construction?
choices: G's vertices as cities; distance 1 for edges, 2 for non-edges; threshold k = n
questions.explanation: Tour of length <= n must use only weight-1 edges, recovering a Hamiltonian cycle in G.

questions.stem: To prove Y is NP-complete, the two-step recipe is:
choices: Show Y in P; pick a known NP-complete X and reduce Y to X
Show Y in NP via a certifier; reduce a known NP-complete X to Y
Show Y is decidable; bound its time
Show Y has a greedy algorithm; reduce to flow
questions.explanation: Always: (1) Y in NP (certifier), (2) NP-hard (X <=_p Y for known NP-complete X).

questions.stem: Which problem is in P?
questions.explanation: Bipartite Matching is solvable by max-flow in O(mn) time. The other three are NP-complete.

questions.stem: Why is NP defined asymmetrically (only yes-certificates)?
choices: No-instances of natural problems often lack short certificates; coNP captures the dual notion
questions.explanation: NP and coNP are distinct (probably); many problems have short yes-certificates but no obvious short no-certificate.

questions.stem: VC <=_p Set Cover uses which encoding?
choices: Universe = edges, sets = vertex incidence sets
questions.explanation: Each vertex induces the set of edges it covers; k-vertex cover iff k-set cover of E.

questions.stem: If P != NP, then:
choices: No NP-complete problem is in P
Every NP problem is in P
questions.explanation: P != NP means NP-complete problems strictly outside P. No polynomial algorithm for any NP-complete.

questions.stem: Which is the typical certificate length bound in NP?
questions.explanation: NP allows polynomial-length certificates; longer would not be polynomially checkable.

questions.stem: If 3-SAT <=_p Subset Sum, then Subset Sum is:
choices: NP-hard (and if Subset Sum is also in NP, NP-complete)
questions.explanation: 3-SAT being NP-complete implies any problem 3-SAT reduces to is NP-hard.

questions.stem: P is a subset of which?
questions.explanation: Every problem in P is in NP (certificate can be empty; algorithm itself is the verifier).

questions.stem: Why does the gadget reduction 3-SAT <=_p Hamiltonian Cycle use 'variable lanes'?
choices: Each lane can be traversed in one of two directions, encoding the variable's truth value, and clause nodes hang off lanes corresponding to satisfied literals
questions.explanation: Direction = truth assignment; consistency across lanes plus correct clause traversal encodes satisfiability.

questions.stem: Subset Sum's NP-hardness reduction from 3-SAT uses what trick to avoid carries?
choices: A base large enough that summed columns never overflow into the next digit
questions.explanation: Large-base construction guarantees independent column behaviour; each column encodes a variable or clause constraint.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a typical way to make a reduction polynomial-time?
choices: Use a constant number of gadgets per variable / clause
Use simple parameter mappings (k -> n - k)
questions.explanation: Exponential construction is not polynomial-time; reductions must finish in polynomial time on input size.

questions.stem: If Y is NP-complete and X <=_p Y, then X is:
questions.explanation: X being reducible to Y says nothing about X's hardness — perhaps X is in P. Reductions transfer hardness from X to Y, not Y to X.

questions.stem: Which problem is the standard 'starting point' for NP-hardness proofs in this unit?
choices: 3-SAT (or sometimes Vertex Cover / Independent Set after the initial chain)
questions.explanation: 3-SAT is the universal starting point; once IS, VC are shown hard, they often serve as more convenient starting points.

questions.stem: A common mistake in reduction proofs is to:
choices: Provide a forward direction without a backward direction (or vice versa)
questions.explanation: Both directions of the iff are necessary. Only-forward shows MAXFLOW >= OBJ but not the other way.

questions.stem: TSP is NP-complete; what is its certifier?
choices: A sequence of cities forming a tour, certifier checks tour-length <= threshold and each city visited once
questions.explanation: Tour is the certificate; verification (each city once, total weight within threshold) is linear.

questions.stem: Which is a correct statement about the relationship between P, NP, and NP-complete?
choices: P, NP, and NP-complete are disjoint
P is a subset of NP; NP-complete is a subset of NP; whether P = NP is open
NP-complete is a subset of P
questions.explanation: P ⊆ NP. NP-complete ⊆ NP. P = NP-complete iff P = NP, which is the open question.

questions.stem: What does Cook-Levin's proof technique amount to, conceptually?
choices: It encodes any polynomial-time certifier's computation as a polynomial-size Boolean circuit; satisfiability of the circuit corresponds to existence of a yes-certificate
questions.explanation: Cook-Levin reduces every NP problem to CIRCUIT-SAT by encoding the certifier's polynomial-time computation as a Boolean circuit on the input + certificate.
